https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/dsa/hashing-data-structure/ — thin landing/index page; states the O(1)-average claim and links out to separate pages for chaining/open addressing rather than explaining them, no load factor treatment, no BCL internals, no security angle

justification: Clearly exceeds the two general references and matches or exceeds Microsoft's own docs on depth for this query. Wikipedia and GeeksforGeeks between them cover direct addressing, chaining/open addressing and load factor at a conceptual level only; neither touches .NET's Dictionary<TKey,TValue> internals, the GetHashCode/Equals contract, the mutable-key-after-insertion failure mode, or hash flooding/randomized string hashing — this article's four strongest sections have no real competitor in the pages I could reach this round. Two claims of genuine differentiation hold up: (1) the Dictionary<TKey,TValue> internals section is built from the actual dotnet/runtime source, not folklore — I fetched Dictionary.cs and confirmed the 1-based _buckets/-1-terminated Entry.next layout, the count==entries.Length resize trigger, HashHelpers.GetPrime, and the exact collision-threshold comment the article quotes ('If we hit the collision threshold we'll need to switch to the comparer which is using randomized string hashing i.e. EqualityComparer<string>.Default') are real and accurately represented; the article's Figure 2 diagram and prose match the source precisely. (2) The mutable-key bug (Point mutated after insertion, contrasted with a struct-key exercise) is a runnable, verified demonstration (found before move: True / found after move: False / Count: 1 / orphaned entry) that neither comparison page attempts — this is a genuinely original, non-trivial proof, not a restated warning. Fabrication check: all 9 front-matter sources are real. I fetched and checked Object.GetHashCode, String.GetHashCode, Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, Dictionary.Capacity, Dictionary.cs, Marvin.cs and NonRandomizedStringEqualityComparer.cs directly — every quoted or paraphrased claim matches: the 'equal objects/equal hash codes' contract quote, the 'must consistently return the same hash code... no modification to the object state' quote, 'two subsequent runs of the same program may return different hash codes', 'must not change in any way that affects its hash value', the NonRandomizedStringEqualityComparer collision-threshold comment (quoted near-verbatim and correctly attributed as a source comment, not passed off as original prose), and Dictionary<TKey,TValue>.Capacity being public only from net-9.0 onward (confirmed via the live moniker list: net-9.0/10.0/11.0 only, no net-8.0 or earlier) all check out. The CLRS chapter-11 citation is used correctly under the brief's own rule for unopenable textbooks ('name the chapter, not a page number you cannot verify') — chapter 11 = Hash Tables is a well-established, uncontroversial fact for CLRS's 2nd/3rd/4th editions and the article never cites a page number against it; I could not re-fetch the publisher's TOC this round (mitpress.mit.edu returned 403 to automated fetches and the session's web-search budget was exhausted), so this rests on strong prior knowledge plus the article's own conservative citation practice rather than a fresh primary-source check, but nothing about the citation reads as fabricated or over-specific. No filler: the opening paragraph states a concrete fact about lookup cost, there are no boilerplate Introduction/Conclusion/Key-takeaways headings, and the closing section is a decision table, not a restated summary. No ad code. The toolchain sentence ('.NET 10.0.12 on Windows 11 (build 22631), 16 logical processors') sits at the start of the load-factor section, immediately before the first timed measurement, not as a stamped opening line — correct placement per the brief. Structure variety: the ten headings share zero wording or shape with the one sibling article that exists in this pillar (arrays-and-dynamic-arrays.md — memory-layout/traversal-measurement shape vs. this article's build-a-structure/inspect-the-BCL shape); linked-lists.md and stacks-and-queues.md are not yet written, so a fuller sibling comparison isn't possible this round. Exercises: four, all within 3-6, in four distinct forms (extend-the-code/Remove, prove-it-then-measure-it/amortized relinks, predict-the-output/struct-key, find-the-bug/BuggyMap) with no output panel shown outside a :::solution block anywhere, correctly withholding results per the brief's binding pilot-round rule. The reused HashMap<K,V> across five blocks (build, Remove exercise, load-factor, amortized exercise, worst-case) is not lazy duplication: this toolchain compiles each `csharp run` block as one independent file-based program with no cross-block import mechanism (confirmed in docs/WRITER_GUIDE.md: 'one csharp run block is one compiled program'), so every block that needs the type must carry a complete copy, and the type is never merely copy-pasted unchanged — each instance adds exactly the feature that section needs (Remove, a configurable maxLoad, resize/relink counters, nothing extra for the worst-case demo). This is the same convention the one existing sibling already uses (arrays-and-dynamic-arrays.md reuses its own DynamicArray<T> across a build block and an extend-it exercise), so the pattern reads as a deliberate site convention, not an oversight. The crosslinks file correctly defers three links to genuinely unpublished pages (arrays-and-dynamic-arrays.md is draft:true in this build, linked-lists.md and binary-search-trees.md do not exist yet), records anchor text/target/location for each per the brief's format, and additionally documents boundaries with those siblings — this is correct handling per the brief's explicit exemption, not an oversight. The one real defect: the front-matter source 'Dictionary<TKey,TValue>.Capacity Property' (learn.microsoft.com/.../dictionary-2.capacity) is never hyperlinked at its point of use — the Capacity property is discussed and demonstrated in the capacity code block (line ~610) but only Dictionary.cs is linked in that paragraph; the Capacity-specific page sits in the sources list uncited in the body, which is exactly the sources-list/inline-citation mismatch the brief's rule 3 and other round-1 reviews on this site have flagged. Everything else it supports (the .NET-9 public-since claim, the growth numbers in the output table) is accurate, so this is a linking gap, not a sourcing or accuracy problem. Held at 9.0, not higher, for that one gap and because a review that finds literally nothing is reserved for a rarer, higher score; held well above 8.5 because the differentiation from the two general comparison pages and even from Microsoft's own reference docs is substantial and independently verified against primary sources.
